anatomy.lede: A sea otter is a weasel remade for the sea: webbed hind feet for swimming, nimble forepaws for handling food, and a coat that does the job other marine mammals leave to blubber.

hotspots.label: Webbed hind feet
hotspots.text: The hind legs are long and the feet broad, flat and webbed. Swimming, the otter tucks in its forelimbs and drives itself with its hind feet and tail.

hotspots.label: Tail
hotspots.text: The flattened tail is less than a third of the body length, about 25–35 cm.

hotspots.label: Whiskers
hotspots.text: Long, sensitive whiskers help it find small animals among kelp and in rock crevices.

hotspots.label: Forepaws
hotspots.text: The short forelimbs have retractable claws and agile paws for grooming and for rubbing, twisting and pulling prey apart.

hotspots.label: Two-layer fur
hotspots.text: A dark underfur lies beneath longer, lighter guard hairs, which trap a layer of air that keeps the skin dry.

senses.lede: Sea otters hunt on the seabed largely by feel, and know one another by smell and voice.

senses.name: Whiskers and paws
senses.text: It searches the dense kelp and crevices with its whiskers and forepaws, catching prey by touch.

senses.name: Smell
senses.text: Each otter has its own scent that conveys identity, age and sex. Yet its genome shows many olfactory receptor genes have decayed, as in other aquatic mammals.

senses.name: Hearing
senses.text: Researchers have recognised nine calls, from the squeals pups use to reach their mothers to coos, growls, snarls and distress screams.

body.lede: Being a small, blubberless mammal in cold water makes life expensive.

systems.title: Fur instead of fat
systems.text: With no insulating fat, the sea otter depends entirely on its fur for warmth, so it grooms meticulously to keep the coat waterproof.

systems.title: A costly lifestyle
systems.text: Measured in captive males, a foraging dive cost nearly twice as much energy as predicted for a seal, partly because the buoyant otter has to work hard to swim down. Wild otters balance this with long rests on the surface.

systems.title: Built-in pockets
systems.text: Loose pouches of skin under the forearms carry a stone tool and food gathered on a dive, leaving the paws free.

systems.title: Water from food
systems.text: It gets most of its water from its prey but also drinks seawater.

genome.lede: Sea otter genomes record both its move into the sea and its brush with extinction.

findings.title: Genes for life at sea
findings.text: Comparisons with the giant otter found signs of natural selection on genes for limb development and hair follicles.

findings.title: Very little diversity
findings.text: Southern and northern sea otters have extremely low genetic diversity and signs of recent inbreeding, raising the burden of possibly harmful mutations.

findings.title: Older declines
findings.text: Population declines visible in the genome may predate the fur trade.

mind.lede: Sea otters are the only marine mammals known to use stones habitually when foraging.

studies.title: Otter archaeology
studies.text: Over ten years at Bennett Slough, California, otters pounded mussels on the same rocks, leaving distinctive wear and heaps of shells broken in a characteristic way.

studies.title: Personal menus
studies.text: Individuals specialise: one otter may eat mostly urchins and crabs while another eats mostly fish, depending on its skills and on what is available.

studies.title: Keeping a tool
studies.text: An otter often keeps the same stone for many dives, carrying it in its forearm pouch.

survival.lede: Life at the surface leaves sea otters exposed to sharks from below and eagles from above.

tactics.title: Anchored in kelp
tactics.text: Resting otters float on their backs and wrap themselves in kelp so they do not drift, often in groups called rafts.

tactics.title: Dive with the pup
tactics.text: At any sign of a predator a mother grips her pup by the neck and dives.

threats.title: Oil spills
threats.text: In California, oil from a single tanker spill could threaten the whole southern population of about 3,000 otters.

threats.title: Shark bites
threats.text: Shark bites are a major cause of death for California's sea otters.

threats.title: A genetic bottleneck
threats.text: Fur-trade hunting left today's populations with very low genetic diversity, which could hamper recovery.

life.lede: A sea otter pup spends its first months riding on its mother's belly.

stages.name: Pregnancy
stages.text: Thanks to delayed implantation the embryo can pause before developing, so pregnancy length varies widely. Births peak in May–June in the Aleutians and January–March in California.

stages.name: Pup
stages.text: A single pup of 1.4–2.3 kg nurses on milk that is 20–25% fat. Its fluffy coat traps so much air that it floats, and the mother wraps it in kelp when she dives.

stages.name: Young otter
stages.text: Pups start diving at about 2 months but rely on their mothers for six to eight months.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Females mature at about 4 years and males at 5–6, though males may not mate until much later. Females usually pup once every one to two years.

lifespan.value: Up to about 23 years in the wild
